guides.title: How to compress a video to 25 MB for Discord
guides.meta_description: Shrink MP4 clips under Discord’s upload limit in your browser. Free video compressor on web-free.site—no sign-up.
steps: Open the Free Video Compressor and load your MP4 or MOV file in the browser.
Pick a target size preset close to 25 MB or lower if Discord still rejects the file.
Start compression and keep the tab open until the progress finishes.
Download the output and check the file size in your file manager before you upload to Discord.

sections.heading: Why Discord rejects large videos
sections.body: Discord caps standard uploads on many accounts at about 25 MB (and less on mobile networks). Compressing locally avoids sending your raw clip to an unknown server and lets you retry presets without waiting on a upload queue.

sections.heading: Quality tips
sections.body: If faces or text look soft, try a slightly higher bitrate preset and compress again. Short screen recordings often shrink dramatically with H.264 or similar browser encoders. Trim dead air first with a cutter tool if the clip is mostly static slides.

faq: Does compression upload my video?
The compressor is built for in-browser work; see the tool privacy note before you process private footage.
What if the file is still over 25 MB?
Lower resolution or trim length, then compress again.

sections.body: Marketplace sellers and freelancers often need one hero image without mailing IDs or inventory shots to a third-party API. Browser-side segmentation keeps the file on your device for that session.

sections.heading: Hard edges and hair
sections.body: Busy hair and glass reflections are never perfect. Zoom in on the preview and touch up stray pixels in a photo editor if the listing must be flawless.

sections.heading: Local cutout vs upload APIs
sections.body: Upload-based services can be excellent on product shots but send pixels off-device. This guide’s tool targets in-browser segmentation—read the hub comparison “background removal vs cloud APIs” before you pick a workflow for a whole catalog.

faq: Can I use the PNG on Etsy or Shopify?
Yes for your own listings; always follow each marketplace’s image rules.
Which format should I export?
PNG preserves transparency; use WebP or JPG after compression for faster page loads.

sections.heading: Why validate before deploy
sections.body: A single trailing comma breaks parsers in production. Formatting in the tab lets you see structure without shipping invalid config.

sections.heading: Secrets hygiene
sections.body: Never paste production API keys on a shared computer. Client-side formatting reduces exposure but does not remove clipboard history—close the tab when finished.

sections.heading: When an IDE is enough
sections.body: If you already work in VS Code, pasting into a `.json` file may be faster. Use this guide’s tool when you are in a ticket, chat log, or dashboard without a project open—see also the hub comparison “JSON formatter vs IDE.”

faq: Does it store my paste?
The formatter is intended for client-side use with no hub account; nothing is saved on the hub.
Can I minify for production?
Yes—minify after you verify the pretty-printed version is correct.

sections.body: Downscale oversized camera photos with Free Image Resizer before compressing—pixels you never display should not ship to visitors. For how browser compression compares to desktop catalogs, read the honest comparison guide on the hub (search “image compressor vs desktop”).
